traveler: Claude-Henri de Rouvroy, comte de Saint-Simon
title: The Canal and the Parable: an Officer of the King Who Invented the Industrial Age
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Paris, birth into the house of Rouvroy
stops.date_confidence: attested; BnF authority record cb11923405t. The exact birth address in Paris is not established in any source consulted, so the coordinate marks the city rather than a house.
stops.campa: Claude-Henri de Rouvroy is born in Paris into the Sandricourt branch of a noble house that counts the memoirist duc de Saint-Simon among its distant kin. The family carries a tradition of descent from Charlemagne through the medieval counts of Vermandois, a line modern genealogists call unproven. The child receives a name that arrives already loaded: a title, a court memoir, an emperor at the far end of the pedigree. Which address in Paris takes him in is not recorded anywhere.
suggested_refs: The BnF authority record for Saint-Simon, catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb11923405t
sources: Richard Swedberg, 'Saint-Simon's vision of a united Europe', European Journal of Sociology

stops.name: Falvy, the estate above the Somme
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The childhood is placed in the 1760s and 1770s by later biography with no contemporary document behind it. The family's tenure of Falvy is separately documented: the commune's list of seigneurs names Balthazar de Saint-Simon Rouvroy in 1780 and Claude Henri de Saint Simon in 1789. Month and day defaulted. Coordinate corrected to the village centre, 49.8250 / 2.9597; an earlier value of 2.9958 lands in farmland east of the houses.
stops.campa: The Rouvroy holdings lie in Picardy on the flat chalk country above the Somme, and the boy passes part of his childhood moving between Paris and the estate at Falvy. The village register of seigneurs will carry his own name against the year 1789. Of the childhood itself almost nothing survives: no schoolbooks, no letters, no tutor's account, no bill. What the documents hold is a name, a village and some fields. The Saint-Simonians will later fill that blank with a boyhood of prodigies and refusals.
suggested_refs: The seigneur list of the commune of Falvy, Somme, naming a Saint-Simon Rouvroy in 1780 and Claude Henri de Saint Simon in 1789
sources: Pierre Musso, biographical reconstruction, as characterized in the research dossier

stops.name: Paris, the tutor who may never have taught him
stops.date_confidence: legend, not documented. The claim that Jean-Jacques Rousseau personally taught the young Saint-Simon runs through the biographical tradition and is judged weakly attested there; no source consulted in this pass confirms it. Retained as tradition and nothing more. Month and day defaulted; the year is a placeholder inside the boyhood.
stops.campa: Tradition puts Jean-Jacques Rousseau in the room, teaching the boy. Nothing supports it. Rousseau is in Paris in these years, copying music by the page and finishing the Confessions, and a family with a Charlemagne story in its pocket might plausibly have wanted him: that is the whole of the case for it. The story is worth keeping for what it shows about the reputation Saint-Simon later attracted, a man to whom the century's teachers get assigned backwards. Whether the two ever met, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: The Rousseau-as-tutor tradition, as transmitted in nineteenth-century Saint-Simonian biography
sources: Research dossier, citing the biographical tradition and flagging it as weakly documented or legendary

stops.name: Paris, the commission in the king's service
stops.date_confidence: contested and unresolved. Saint-Simon's own later account and Pierre Musso's reconstruction give January 1777; an Encyclopedia of the American Revolution entry gives 1775 instead. No muster roll was consulted that settles it. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: He enters the royal service as an officer before his seventeenth birthday, in the ordinary way of his class: purchase, patronage, a family that has been handing sons to the crown for centuries. He is made a captain of cavalry. The dates do not agree, one tradition putting the commission in 1775 and another in January 1777, and nothing consulted here decides between them. The first thing the boy with the Charlemagne pedigree becomes is a junior officer with a horse.
suggested_refs: Pierre Musso's reconstruction of the 1777 enlistment, against the 1775 date carried in American Revolution military reference works
sources: Pierre Musso, biographical reconstruction, as characterized in the research dossier
Encyclopedia of the American Revolution, military service entry (conflicting date)

stops.name: Brest, sailing for the Caribbean
stops.date_confidence: attested for the regiment and the port; the exact sailing date is not established and the month is a placeholder. The 'age seventeen' gloss carried in some reference entries is impossible for a 1779 embarkation: born 17 October 1760, he is eighteen through most of that year. Seventeen belongs to the enlistment, not to this crossing.
stops.campa: He transfers out of the cavalry into the Regiment de Touraine and sails from Brest, the Atlantic arsenal behind Vauban's old works, for the Caribbean theatre of the American war. The regiment will carry Martinique and Yorktown among its battle honours. He is eighteen. France has entered the war on the American side and is fighting it the way France always fights Britain, in the sugar islands as much as on the continent, and the road to Virginia runs through the West Indies.
suggested_refs: The battle honours of the Regiment de Touraine, listing Yorktown and Martinique 1780
sources: New World Encyclopedia, 'Henri de Saint-Simon' (military service)

stops.name: Cap-Francais, the sugar colony
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Military-reference chronology places the regiment in the French Caribbean; no landing port or date is documented in the sources consulted. The coordinate is Cap-Francais, the colony's principal port, used as a landmark stand-in. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: The regiment reaches the French Atlantic empire at its richest point, Saint-Domingue, the sugar and coffee colony whose enslaved population produces more wealth than any other holding France owns. The young officer sees a productive system running at full speed on forced labour, and there is nothing in forty years of his writing on industry that says he found it worth remarking. What the record shows is the port itself, from which the fleets stage: a garrison, a harbour, ships fitting out for the north.
suggested_refs: The port of Cap-Francais, staging point of French Caribbean operations in the American war
sources: Research dossier, military-reference synthesis (no exact landing site named)

stops.name: Barbados, the coalition war in the islands
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Military summaries connect him with operations around Barbados; no specific engagement was independently verified in this pass, and the phrasing follows the cautious wording of the underlying source. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Military summaries connect him with operations around Barbados during the coalition war against Britain, in a theatre where hurricanes wreck more ships than gunfire and fever kills more men than both together. Whatever he does in 1780 he does as a line officer under other men's orders, inside a strategic argument that Britain can be beaten by taking its islands rather than its colonies. That argument is settled the following year on a Virginia river. No engagement of his own is named anywhere.
suggested_refs: French Caribbean operations of 1780, the year between Saint-Domingue and the Chesapeake
sources: Research dossier, characterization of military-reference material (unverified beyond the dossier)

stops.name: Yorktown, the guns before the surrender
stops.date_confidence: attested for the siege and the surrender date. His personal role, commanding his regiment's gunners, rests on military-reference tradition rather than a muster document. The marquis Claude-Anne de Rouvroy de Saint-Simon-Montblery, an older relative who commanded some 3,500 men at this same siege, is routinely confused with him; that material is excluded here. Coordinate is the corpus pin for Yorktown.
stops.campa: The allied lines close on Cornwallis between the York River and the siege works, and the Regiment de Touraine is in them. Accounts credit the young Saint-Simon with commanding his regiment's gunners while the batteries walk their fire in toward the British redoubts. On the nineteenth of October the garrison marches out to surrender. A different Rouvroy de Saint-Simon, an older relative commanding thousands in the same army on the same field, is mistaken for him in the reference books to this day.
suggested_refs: The Yorktown siege lines of September and October 1781
The American Revolution Institute's account of the marquis de Saint-Simon-Montblery, the older relative with whom he is confused
sources: New World Encyclopedia, 'Henri de Saint-Simon' (captain of artillery at Yorktown)

stops.name: The Chesapeake, sailing south with de Grasse
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The withdrawal of de Grasse's fleet from the Chesapeake is documented; the officer's presence aboard follows the military-reference chronology. The coordinate approximates the mouth of the bay, no exact departure point being named in the sources.
stops.campa: Two weeks after the surrender the French fleet weighs and stands out of the Chesapeake for the Caribbean, past the same capes it closed against the British navy in September. The North American war is effectively finished; the war in the islands is not. Ahead of the fleet is a British fortress built up the side of a dead volcano on St Kitts. Saint-Simon sails with de Grasse, an officer with a successful siege behind him and no particular prospect beyond the next station. He is twenty-one years old.
suggested_refs: The departure of de Grasse's fleet from the Chesapeake, November 1781

stops.name: Brimstone Hill, the fortress on the volcanic rock
stops.date_confidence: attested. The French siege opens 11 January 1782 and the British garrison surrenders after about a month, on 12 February. A narrower dating of 'February 1782' carried in some summaries is too tight; the stop is dated to the opening of the siege.
stops.campa: The French land on St Kitts on the eleventh of January and lay siege to Brimstone Hill, the British fortress raised eight hundred feet up the flank of a dead volcano and mounting guns that can reach the anchorage below. Saint-Simon is in the siege works, at the second fortified position he has watched give way in four months. It is also the last one that will give way in his favour. The garrison holds out a month, cut off, outnumbered, Nevis already gone, and marches out on the twelfth of February.
suggested_refs: Brimstone Hill Fortress, St Kitts, besieged 11 January to 12 February 1782
sources: Wikipedia, 'Brimstone Hill Fortress National Park' (siege dates)

stops.name: The Saintes Passage, the line broken
stops.date_confidence: attested for the battle and its date; his presence in the French fleet and his capture follow the biographical tradition carried in the standard reference entries.
stops.campa: Rodney's ships break the French line in the passage between Dominica and Guadeloupe, take de Grasse's flagship with the admiral still aboard her, and end at a stroke the Franco-Spanish plan to invade Jamaica. Saint-Simon is inside the wreck of it and is captured. The fleet that carried him out of the Chesapeake in November is scattered by the second week of April, and the officer who stood in the winning siege works at Yorktown six months ago is now cargo on a British deck.
suggested_refs: The Battle of the Saintes, 9 to 12 April 1782, and the capture of the Ville de Paris

stops.name: Kingston, prisoner of war
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was held in Jamaica as a prisoner of war until the 1783 peace. No place of detention on the island is named in the sources consulted; the coordinate marks Kingston as a landmark stand-in. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: He is taken to Jamaica, the island his own fleet had been assembled to conquer, and held there until the peace of 1783 lets him go. It is the first long idleness of his life. Prisoners in this war are handled by rank and exchanged by ledger, so the months pass without event: a hot colony, nothing to command, nothing to read but what he is handed, and a great deal of time in which to consider what a cut between two oceans would be worth. He comes out at twenty-two with the war over and a canal in his head.
suggested_refs: British prisoner-of-war administration in Jamaica, 1782 to 1783

stops.name: Mexico City, the canal laid before the viceroy
stops.date_confidence: the canal proposal is corroborated by the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica independently of the dossier's biographical tradition. No engineering dossier and no viceregal reply have been located, and the date within 1783 is not fixed. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Released, he does not go home. He crosses to New Spain and puts before the viceroy a plan to cut a canal between the Atlantic and the Pacific, a scheme Spanish engineers have raised and shelved for two centuries. Nothing comes of it. No dossier survives, no reply is recorded, and a twenty-two-year-old ex-prisoner has no standing whatever to propose continental engineering to the government of Charles III. He will spend the next forty years doing versions of exactly this.
suggested_refs: The viceregal palace of New Spain, seat of the government he petitioned
1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Saint-Simon, Claude Henri de Rouvroy, Comte de', on the interoceanic canal scheme

stops.name: Mezieres, the garrison and the engineering school
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. He is attached to the regiment d'Aquitaine at Mezieres after 1783 and the biographical tradition places him in the orbit of the Ecole Royale du Genie there; formal enrolment is not established. A frequently repeated link to Gaspard Monge does not belong at this stop: Monge left Mezieres in 1783, while Saint-Simon was still a prisoner in Jamaica. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Back in France he is posted to Mezieres on the Meuse, garrison town of the Ecole Royale du Genie, the school teaching the French army how to build. He is an infantry officer among engineers. What he takes away is not a diploma but a habit of mind: that a road, a lock, a fortification and a state are problems of one kind, and that the men who can solve the first three ought to be handed the fourth. Everything he writes after 1802 is that sentence being restated.
suggested_refs: The Ecole Royale du Genie at Mezieres, the eighteenth century's foremost military engineering school
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Henri de Saint-Simon' (regiment d'Aquitaine at Mezieres after 1783)
Wikipedia, 'Gaspard Monge' (departure from Mezieres in 1783, correcting the usual gloss)

stops.name: Amsterdam, the water country
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Biographical tradition places him in the Netherlands in the mid-1780s; no city, document, or date is established, and the coordinate is Amsterdam as a generic landmark. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Biography sends him to the Netherlands in the middle of the decade, watching a republic come apart and, true to the pattern, watching the water. The Dutch have made a country out of hydraulic administration: dikes, polders, drainage boards, canals that are also roads and also boundaries and also the tax base. It is the nearest thing in Europe to a nation organized as an engineering work, and it is run by boards of men who know how water behaves. No letter or passport puts him in any particular town.
suggested_refs: Dutch hydraulic administration of the 1780s, the polder boards and canal networks
sources: Research dossier, synthesis of biographical tradition (no primary document located)

stops.name: Madrid, the Guadarrama canal
stops.date_confidence: attested that he involved himself in Spanish hydraulic development tied to the Canal del Guadarrama project and the Banco de San Carlos; he was not the system's designer, and the sources are careful to describe his role as entrepreneurial. The window runs 1787 to 1789. Month and day defaulted; the coordinate is central Madrid as a landmark stand-in.
stops.campa: In Spain he attaches himself to the great unfinished work of the Bourbon administration, the canal meant to carry Guadarrama water down toward Madrid and onward to the sea, and to the Banco de San Carlos that is supposed to pay for it. He is a promoter, not the designer. At one point he expects to have thousands of labourers under his direction. Then France begins to come apart, and every project in Europe running on French credit stops where it stands. The canal is never finished.
suggested_refs: The Canal del Guadarrama, the Bourbon hydraulic project he attached himself to
The Banco de San Carlos, financier of the scheme
sources: Spanish infrastructure history of the Canal del Guadarrama (independently documented)

stops.name: Paris, the count becomes Bonhomme
stops.date_confidence: attested that he endorsed the Revolution in 1789 and used revolutionary names including Claude Bonhomme; the precise date of the change is not established and the month is a placeholder. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: He comes home to a country abolishing his class and accepts the abolition without visible struggle. The particle goes, the title goes, and for a time he signs himself Claude Bonhomme, plain fellow. In the village of Falvy his name still stands in the seigneur's column for that same year. He gives up nothing he needs. The Revolution is selling the church and the emigration at auction, and a man with credit, nerve and a Prussian partner can buy a great deal of France very cheaply.
suggested_refs: The pseudonym Claude Bonhomme, adopted in the Revolutionary years
sources: Wikipedia, 'Henri de Saint-Simon' (endorsement of revolutionary ideals, 1789)

stops.name: Notre-Dame, the roof as an asset
stops.date_confidence: the partnership with Redern and the speculation in biens nationaux are attested. The specific scheme to buy the cathedral roof for its metal, sometimes attached to Talleyrand's name, is reported in modern scholarship; it is not established that it was executed, and Talleyrand's part is uncertain. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: With Jean Sigismond Ehrenreich, comte de Redern, a Prussian nobleman with capital, he goes into the biens nationaux: confiscated church land and emigre estates, bought at assignat prices and resold. The cathedral stands over a city in which everything, the cathedral included, now has a price. One reported scheme, sometimes attached to Talleyrand's name, is to purchase the roof of Notre-Dame outright for the value of its metal. Whether that was ever executed is not established.
suggested_refs: The sale of the biens nationaux, 1790 to 1794, and the assignat market that made the fortunes
sources: Oxford intellectual history research on Saint-Simon's technocratic internationalism, as characterized in the research dossier

stops.name: Sainte-Pelagie, arrested under the Terror
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was arrested in 1793 on suspicion of counter-revolutionary activity and held first at Sainte-Pelagie; the exact date of arrest is not established. The month follows the 'roughly eleven months' figure carried in the tradition and is a placeholder. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: The name catches up with him. An ex-count speculating in confiscated property alongside a Prussian partner is precisely the profile the Committee of General Security is arresting. Nothing in particular saves or condemns him: he is one file among thousands in a system not examining files carefully. His partner is abroad, the property deals sit unresolved, and the man who bought half a countryside is in a cell in the fifth arrondissement. He is taken to Sainte-Pelagie in the autumn of 1793.
suggested_refs: Sainte-Pelagie prison, Paris, holding place of suspects under the general-security measures of 1793
sources: Wikipedia, 'Henri de Saint-Simon' (imprisonment on suspicion of counter-revolutionary activities)
Jean Dautry's archival study, as characterized in the research dossier

stops.name: The Luxembourg, Charlemagne at the bedside
stops.date_confidence: the imprisonment and the transfer to the Luxembourg are attested; the release date is not. French sources say only that he left prison after 9 Thermidor, 27 July 1794; English sources say he was released in 1794 at the Terror's end. A precise date of 28 August 1794 circulates but is unsupported and cannot be squared with the 'roughly eleven months' figure carried alongside it. Dated here to the day after 9 Thermidor as the earliest defensible marker. The Charlemagne vision is Saint-Simon's own later self-report and is unverifiable.
stops.campa: Transferred to the Luxembourg, he waits out the Terror in the palace the Revolution has turned into a prison. He will say afterwards that his ancestor Charlemagne came to him in the night here and told him he would equal the emperor's glory in philosophy as the emperor had reached it in politics. Nobody else witnesses this. Thermidor opens the doors and he walks out having spent something near a year inside, poorer, older, and now holding a mandate no one can check.
suggested_refs: The Luxembourg Palace in its brief use as a Revolutionary prison
The Charlemagne vision as transmitted through Olinde Rodrigues's 1832 posthumous edition

stops.name: Palais-Royal, the mansion and the salon
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The household detail, some twenty servants and a mansion near the Palais-Royal, comes from modern correspondence-based scholarship (Musso's 2025 edition of the letters); the salon and the scale of the establishment are traditional. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: The speculation has made him rich and he lives like it: a mansion near the Palais-Royal, some twenty servants, a table laid every day for anybody in Paris who can teach him something. The Directory's Paris is full of people who need a dinner and know something worth knowing. Mathematicians, physiologists, chemists, bankers and engineers come to eat, and he interrogates them about their disciplines like a man assembling a machine out of parts he has to buy one at a time.
stops.quote: Remember, monsieur le comte, that you have great things to do.
stops.quote_source: The formula his valet is said to have used to wake him each morning; reported in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Saint-Simon, Claude Henri de Rouvroy, Comte de', and repeated in the English Wikipedia article citing Donald F. Busky. No contemporary document carries it.
suggested_refs: Pierre Musso, ed., Saint-Simon: Correspondance 1782-1825 (Manucius, 2025), the letters behind the household detail
sources: Research dossier, citing Musso's correspondence-based reconstruction

stops.name: Paris, the quarrel with Redern
stops.date_confidence: attested that the partnership collapsed into an acrimonious dispute over the division of profits and property; the terms of settlement were not verified in this pass. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The partnership ends badly. Redern and Saint-Simon fall out over the division of what they made together in the years of the land sales, and the quarrel is bitter enough to have generated its own small scholarly literature two centuries later. Saint-Simon comes out of it with a great deal less than he went in with. He keeps spending as though he had not. The salon runs on; the arithmetic underneath the salon has changed, and there is no sign anywhere that he looked at it.
suggested_refs: The dedicated older scholarship on the Saint-Simon and Redern dispute
sources: Research dossier, citing specialist literature on the Redern dispute

stops.name: Montagne Sainte-Genevieve, the re-education
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from modern scholarship on the 1798 self-education programme; day-to-day attendance at either school is not documented. Gaspard Monge is teaching descriptive geometry in the Polytechnique's orbit in these years, which is where the frequently misplaced Monge connection actually belongs. Month and day defaulted; the coordinate approximates the Quartier Latin site of the school in this era.
stops.campa: At thirty-eight he decides he has not been educated and sets out to repair it, taking lodgings by the Ecole Polytechnique and following the mathematics and physics on offer there, then moving down toward the Ecole de Medecine for physiology. Gaspard Monge is teaching descriptive geometry in this quarter. The programme is not curiosity. He wants to know exactly how far the physical sciences have got, so that he can build the missing one: a science of man on the same footing, with the same right to be believed. No register at either school records him in it.
suggested_refs: The Ecole Polytechnique in the Quartier Latin, c. 1798, and Monge's course in descriptive geometry
sources: Research dossier, synthesis of Musso and Swedberg scholarship on the 1798 programme

stops.name: Paris, the marriage arranged for the salon
stops.date_confidence: attested for the marriage date, 7 August 1801, and for a divorce within about a year, in 1802. The reported motive, that he married in order to obtain a hostess capable of gathering leading minds, comes from the biographical tradition. The Madame de Stael anecdote comes from Leon Halevy's recollections published in 1832, seven years after Saint-Simon's death, and is not documentary.
stops.campa: He marries Alexandrine-Sophie Goury de Champgrand, a writer who will publish as Sophie de Bawr, and gives as his reason that a philosopher needs a wife who can hold a salon. She is entirely capable of it. The marriage lasts about a year. A story survives that he meant afterwards to propose to Madame de Stael, on the ground that the finest mind in Europe ought to be matched with the finest man in it; the story reaches us from a secretary's recollections published seven years after he was dead.
suggested_refs: Leon Halevy's 1832 recollections, source of the Stael anecdote
sources: New World Encyclopedia, 'Henri de Saint-Simon' (marriage, August 1801)
Research dossier, flagging the Stael anecdote as recollection, not documented fact

stops.name: Geneva, an inhabitant writes to his contemporaries
stops.date_confidence: the imprint is effectively undated and the year is contested. The BnF holds records dated both 1802 and 1803, the Gallica-digitised copy being the 1803 one; most modern scholarship and the New World Encyclopedia date it 1803, while English Wikipedia and the 1911 Britannica give 1802. Dated here to 1803 with the conflict left standing. The pseudonymous persona is independently documented by the BnF author form 'Habitant de Geneve, Un'. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Divorced and travelling, he publishes his first real book behind a mask: Lettres d'un habitant de Geneve a ses contemporains, signed by an inhabitant of Geneva. It proposes that humanity subscribe to a fund at the tomb of Newton, elect twenty-one scientists and artists to administer it, and consent to be governed by them. The same pamphlet argues that Africans cannot be raised by education to the intellectual level of Europeans. The science of man arrives with a racial hierarchy already installed in it.
stops.quote: The revolutionaries applied the principles of equality to negroes. If they had consulted the physiologists they would have learned that the negro, because of his basic physical structure, is not susceptible, even with the same education, of rising to the intellectual level of Europeans.
stops.quote_source: Quoted in English on the English Wikipedia article on Saint-Simon and attributed there to his Lettres, the work left unspecified; not checked in this pass against a named critical edition or translator.
suggested_refs: The BnF author form 'Habitant de Geneve, Un', documenting the pseudonym
The suppressed racial-hierarchy passage in the Lettres, as it circulates in English translation
sources: New World Encyclopedia, 'Henri de Saint-Simon' (1803 dating)

stops.name: London, the travelling years
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Biographies place him in England during post-divorce travels through Britain, Germany and Switzerland; no itinerary, address, or document survives, and the month is a placeholder. The stop is retained as a gap held open on a documented travel arc.
stops.campa: Biographies send him across Britain and the German states in these years, looking, as always, at works: manufactures, ports, machines. England in 1803 is the only country on earth where the thing he will spend the rest of his life theorising already exists in bulk, an economy arranged around production rather than around land and rank. What survives is the shape of a journey he is said to have made and nothing inside it. No letter puts him in any particular English town.
suggested_refs: The English manufacturing districts of 1803, the working model behind his later industrialism
sources: Research dossier, synthesis of biographical tradition (no primary source located)

stops.name: Paris, addressing the scientific state
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. A text on social organization addressed to the chemist and educational administrator Antoine-Francois de Fourcroy is recorded in the bibliography; the exact meeting place is not established. Reported appeals reaching toward Napoleon are petitionary, and no audience or meeting is documented. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He writes to Antoine-Francois de Fourcroy, chemist and reorganizer of French education, and to whatever other officer of the scientific state will read him. He is asking the institutions of the Empire to underwrite a reorganization of all human knowledge, proposed by a divorced ex-count with no post, no degree and a shrinking bank balance. Tradition has the appeals eventually reaching toward Napoleon himself, always as petition, never as audience. Nothing is granted.
suggested_refs: The 1804 letter to Fourcroy on social organization
sources: Research dossier, bibliographic synthesis of the 1804 letter to Fourcroy
napoleon.journey.json (petitionary relation only; no meeting documented)

stops.name: Paris, mapping the labour of the sciences
stops.date_confidence: the work is dated 1803 by English Wikipedia and 1807 by the BnF catalogue, which records the printing by J.-L. Scherff in Paris, in quarto, pages 1 to 176. The BnF imprint is followed here and the conflict is left standing. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Introduction aux travaux scientifiques du dix-neuvieme siecle sets out to survey the entire labour of the sciences and then redistribute it, giving every discipline its assigned place inside one division of intellectual work, with physiology raised to the rank the physical sciences already hold. J.-L. Scherff prints it in Paris, in quarto, a hundred and seventy-six pages. The catalogues cannot even agree on the year it appeared, 1803 in one and 1807 in another. Almost nobody reads it.
suggested_refs: BnF record for Introduction aux travaux scientifiques du dix-neuvieme siecle, Paris, Impr. de J.-L. Scherff, 1807, ark:/12148/cb31285237m
sources: Wikipedia, 'Henri de Saint-Simon' (1803 dating, in conflict)

stops.name: The Mont-de-Piete, the copyist
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the older Larousse biographical tradition; no employment record was located in this pass. The Diard episode rests on the same standard accounts and no address for Diard's lodging is established. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: The money is gone. He takes a copyist's desk at the Mont-de-Piete, the municipal pawnshop, and earns a clerk's wage inside the institution where the poor of Paris turn their possessions into a few francs. Ten years earlier he kept twenty servants a mile from here. He goes on writing about the organization of industry throughout. When even the copying fails, a former servant of his own named Diard takes him in and feeds him. No employment record for the copying survives.
suggested_refs: The Mont-de-Piete on the rue des Blancs-Manteaux, the municipal pawnshop of Paris
sources: Research dossier, citing the older Larousse biographical tradition
Research dossier, standard accounts of the Diard relationship

stops.name: Paris, the letter to Dumeril
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from a FranceArchives manuscript catalogue record of a letter from Saint-Simon to Dumeril dated 6 November 1813; the letter's contents were not read in this pass and the place of composition is not given, so the general Paris coordinate is used.
stops.campa: He writes to Andre Marie Constant Dumeril, physician and naturalist, about the manuscript he is calling his Memoire sur la science de l'homme. The letter survives in a French archive catalogue. It matters for a plain reason: it puts him inside a real scientific correspondence of his own century, addressing a working naturalist, rather than only inside the collected editions his disciples assembled after his death out of what they wished he had written.
stops.quote: The philosopher places himself at the summit of thought; from there he views what the world has been and what it must become.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Saint-Simon, Science de l'homme: Physiologie religieuse, in the posthumous edition of 1858; English wording as carried on Wikiquote, translator unnamed. The volume is a compiled posthumous text and the sentence carries that caution.
suggested_refs: FranceArchives catalogue record of the Saint-Simon letter to Dumeril, 6 November 1813
sources: FranceArchives (francearchives.gouv.fr) catalogue record, as characterized in the research dossier

stops.name: Paris, Thierry and the reorganization of Europe
stops.date_confidence: attested; the BnF catalogue entry for the 1814 work carries both names on the title page. The place of composition is not specified in the sources consulted, so the general Paris coordinate is used. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Europe is being redrawn at Vienna by the powers who have just beaten Napoleon, and Saint-Simon, with the young historian Augustin Thierry as secretary and co-author, publishes a rival plan: a common parliament above the nations, each nation keeping its independence, the whole built on an Anglo-French pairing. It is the first serious European federation scheme of the modern era, and it is written by a man living on charity. The parliament it proposes is assigned a task, and the task is colonizing the world.
stops.quote: To colonize the world with the European race, which is superior to every other race: to make the world accessible and habitable like Europe—such is the sort of enterprise by which the European Parliament should continually keep Europe active and happy.
stops.quote_source: De la reorganisation de la societe europeenne (1814), written with Augustin Thierry; English wording as quoted in Richard Swedberg, 'Saint-Simon's vision of a united Europe', European Journal of Sociology (Cambridge University Press).
suggested_refs: BnF record for De la reorganisation de la societe europeenne, Paris, 1814
Richard Swedberg, 'Saint-Simon's vision of a united Europe', European Journal of Sociology
sources: BnF catalogue entry for the 1814 work
Richard Swedberg, European Journal of Sociology

stops.name: The Arsenal, a post he may not have held
stops.date_confidence: unresolved contradiction, not adjudicated here. The older Larousse tradition has him aligning with Benjamin Constant during the Hundred Days and holding a librarian's post at the Bibliotheque de l'Arsenal, lost after Waterloo. Saint-Simon's own 1821 letter to Robin Scevole claims he accepted no government office after 1789. Both statements cannot straightforwardly be true and neither is dropped. Month is a placeholder inside the Hundred Days; day defaulted.
stops.campa: Napoleon comes back from Elba and Paris changes hands again inside a week. Tradition puts Saint-Simon among Benjamin Constant's people through the Hundred Days and gives him a librarian's post at the Bibliotheque de l'Arsenal, which Waterloo takes away three months later. Six years afterwards, in a letter to Robin Scevole, he writes that he has accepted no place from any government since 1789. One of those two statements is false and the record does not say which.
suggested_refs: Saint-Simon's 1821 letter to Robin Scevole, denying any government office since 1789
The Bibliotheque de l'Arsenal, the post the Larousse tradition assigns him
sources: Research dossier, citing the older Larousse tradition against Saint-Simon's own 1821 letter

stops.name: Paris, L'Industrie
stops.date_confidence: attested for the periodical, issued in irregular cahiers from late 1816 onward; New World Encyclopedia dates it 1817 while the dossier's bibliographic synthesis puts the launch in December 1816. The exact day is a placeholder and no publishing address was established.
stops.campa: He begins issuing L'Industrie in irregular instalments, and with it the sentence that reorganizes the century's politics: the real division in a society is not noble against commoner but productive against idle. The restored monarchy has just put the idle back in charge of France, which is exactly why the argument lands. Bankers, manufacturers, farmers, engineers and workmen stand on one side. Rentiers, courtiers and the whole apparatus of inherited place stand on the other.
stops.quote: Politics is the science of production.
stops.quote_source: Saint-Simon, De l'industrie (1816); English wording as carried on the Wikiquote page for Henri de Saint-Simon, translator uncredited.
suggested_refs: The cahiers of L'Industrie, 1816 to 1818

stops.name: Paris, Comte at the desk
stops.date_confidence: attested for the collaboration. Reference entries date the working partnership from the L'Organisateur period of 1819, while the specialist literature on the relationship gives the start as approximately 1817, which is followed here. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: A nineteen-year-old expelled from the Ecole Polytechnique presents himself as a secretary and is taken on. Auguste Comte will spend seven years in this room, writing under Saint-Simon's name and, increasingly, writing Saint-Simon's arguments better than Saint-Simon writes them. The pairing is fruitful and unequal in both directions at once: the old man supplies the programme, the young one the rigour, and neither will afterwards admit how much he took.
stops.quote: Today, for the first time since the existence of societies it is a question of organizing a totally new system; of replacing the celestial with the terrestrial, the vague by the positive, and the poetic by the real.
stops.quote_source: Saint-Simon, L'Industrie, as quoted in the contemporary periodical L'Ami de la Religion et du Roi, no. 336, 29 October 1817; English wording as carried on Wikiquote.
suggested_refs: Michel Bourdeau's study of the Saint-Simon and Comte relationship and its rupture
sources: Michel Bourdeau's study, as characterized in the research dossier

stops.name: Paris, the Parable
stops.date_confidence: attested for the August 1819 prospectus and for instalments running into 1820. The label 'Parabole de Saint-Simon' was fixed later, by Olinde Rodrigues's 1832 edition; the passage was not published as a standalone pamphlet in 1819. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: A prospectus goes out for L'Organisateur, and in the instalments that follow he sets down the arithmetic that will be quoted for two hundred years. Suppose France loses in a single night its fifty best physicists, chemists, engineers, bankers, farmers and craftsmen: the nation becomes a body without a soul and needs a generation to recover. Suppose instead it loses the king's brother, the dukes, the marshals, the bishops and ten thousand of the richest proprietors. France grieves, and nothing whatever stops working.
stops.quote: In the old system Society is governed essentially by men; in the new it is governed only by principles.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Saint-Simon, L'Organisateur, cited as 'Org, IV, 197' on the Wikiquote page for Henri de Saint-Simon; translator unnamed.
suggested_refs: fr.wikisource, 'Parabole de Saint-Simon' and the text of L'Organisateur

stops.name: The Palais de Justice, acquitted by a jury
stops.date_confidence: the prosecution following the assassination of the duc de Berry and the acquittal are corroborated in outline by the publication history of L'Organisateur; the precise acquittal date of 23 March 1820 comes from a modern historical summary and is a reconstruction. A second, separate arrest in June 1820 over protest against the 'double vote' electoral law is placed there by the older Larousse tradition and is not independently confirmed. The venue coordinate approximates the Ile de la Cite law courts.
stops.campa: The duc de Berry is assassinated in February and the government moves against anyone who has written that the royal family is dispensable. The Parable is read back to Saint-Simon in court as an incitement. He publishes his defence as an open letter to the jurors, and on the twenty-third of March the assize court acquits him. Three months later he is briefly arrested again in the agitation over the double-vote law, on a charge with no connection to the first.
suggested_refs: Lettres de Henri Saint-Simon a MM. les jures (1820), his printed defence
sources: Research dossier, modern historical summary of the trial and acquittal date
Research dossier, citing the older Larousse tradition for the June 1820 arrest

segments.name: The Pistol and the Last Book

stops.name: Paris, Du systeme industriel
stops.date_confidence: attested for the work, published in multiple parts from 1821. Month and day defaulted. The formula about the administration of things replacing the government of men is a later crystallization of arguments present in these pages, principally by Friedrich Engels, and is not a verbatim sentence of Saint-Simon's.
stops.campa: Du systeme industriel comes out in parts and states the thesis flat: industry is the decisive fact of the age, and political institutions must be rebuilt around the men who produce. Government over persons is to give way to the administration of things. He never writes that sentence in that form. Engels will assemble it out of these pages sixty years later and hand it to the socialist movement as a slogan, where it outruns everything Saint-Simon actually published.
stops.quote: True equality consists in each drawing benefits from society in exact proportion to his social outlay, that is to his real capacity, to the beneficent use he makes of his abilities.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Saint-Simon, Systeme industriel, cited as 'Syst. Indus, VI, 17' on the Wikiquote page for Henri de Saint-Simon; translator unnamed.
suggested_refs: Friedrich Engels, Socialism: Utopian and Scientific (1880), Part I, the later reading that gave these pages their slogan
sources: New World Encyclopedia, 'Henri de Saint-Simon' (Du systeme industriel, 1821)
Friedrich Engels, Socialism: Utopian and Scientific (1880), marxists.org

stops.name: Paris, the pistol
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and for the loss of sight in one eye. The exact address is not established in the sources consulted, so the general Paris coordinate is used. A widely repeated detail that he fired six shots is unverified and is excluded. Olinde Rodrigues's support from this point rests on the general biographical tradition, corroborated by his well-documented editorial role after 1825.
stops.campa: On the ninth of March he puts a pistol to his head and fires. He lives. The ball takes the sight of one eye and leaves him alive at sixty-two, destitute, in a rented room, the work unread and the money forty years gone. Out of the wreck comes the last support of his life: Olinde Rodrigues, mathematician and financier, attaches himself to him after the attempt and keeps him fed through the two years remaining. It is Rodrigues who will afterwards decide what Saint-Simon meant.
suggested_refs: Olinde Rodrigues, the mathematician and financier who sustained him from 1823 and edited him from 1825

stops.name: Paris, the Catechisme des industriels
stops.date_confidence: attested for the work, issued in cahiers across 1823 and 1824, and for the third cahier being substantially Auguste Comte's own writing. The month is a placeholder inside the publication run; day defaulted.
stops.campa: The Catechisme des industriels appears in cahiers through 1823 and 1824 and does what its title claims: it tells the industriels who they are. Not a class defined by property but by function, everybody who makes or moves or grows or finances anything, set against everybody who lives on what others make. The third cahier is essentially Comte's own writing, printed under Saint-Simon's name. It is over that cahier that seven years in the same room come apart.
stops.quote: The whole of society rests upon industry.
stops.quote_source: Saint-Simon, L'Industrie, reprinted in Oeuvres de Saint-Simon, vol. 18 (1868); English wording as carried on the Wikiquote page for Henri de Saint-Simon, translator unnamed.
suggested_refs: The third cahier of the Catechisme des industriels, substantially written by Auguste Comte
sources: Wikipedia and New World Encyclopedia, both dating the Catechisme des industriels 1823 to 1824

stops.name: Paris, the break with Comte
stops.date_confidence: attested that the collaboration broke down in 1824 over priority, editorial control, and the divergence between political and spiritual reorganization; the month is a placeholder and the day is defaulted. Leon Halevy's arrival as final secretary is placed in the same year by the biographical tradition, and his 1832 memoir is the source of many later anecdotes.
stops.campa: It ends in the ordinary way, over whose name goes on the title page and whose ideas are whose. Comte wants the positive philosophy with no religion in it; Saint-Simon is turning toward the poor and toward a stripped Christianity that will do the work of moral cohesion. Leon Halevy takes the empty chair and becomes the last secretary, the man who will later supply most of the anecdotes anyone tells about the old man. Comte leaves, and spends the rest of his life minimizing what he owed to this room.
suggested_refs: Leon Halevy's 1832 recollections of Saint-Simon, the major posthumous anecdote source
sources: New World Encyclopedia, 'Henri de Saint-Simon' (the final quarrel)
Michel Bourdeau's study, as characterized in the research dossier

stops.name: Paris, Nouveau Christianisme
stops.date_confidence: attested for the work and for the year 1825, published by Bossange pere and left unfinished. The month of April is carried in the biographical tradition but is not supported by the BnF record, which gives the year only; day defaulted. Note that a BnF ark sometimes cited for this work, cb31285237m, in fact belongs to the 1807 Introduction aux travaux scientifiques and has been double-assigned in circulating source lists.
stops.campa: The last book is a dialogue between a conservative and an innovator. It throws out the theology, the priesthood and the dogma and keeps one commandment: that men are to treat one another as brothers, which means organizing society for the benefit of the poorest class. He has spent twenty-five years arguing that the scientists should govern; he finishes by arguing that they should govern for the poor, and that this is what Christianity was for all along. Bossange pere prints the first dialogue in 1825. There is no second dialogue.
stops.quote: The whole of society ought to strive towards the amelioration of the moral and physical existence of the poorest class; society ought to organize itself in the way best adapted for attaining this end.
stops.quote_source: Saint-Simon, Nouveau Christianisme (1825), English rendering as given in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica and, word for word, in the English Wikipedia article; translator uncredited in both.
suggested_refs: Nouveau christianisme, dialogues entre un conservateur et un novateur. Premier dialogue, Paris, Bossange pere, 1825
sources: BnF catalogue record for the 1825 Bossange edition

stops.name: 9 rue du Faubourg-Montmartre, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and for Paris. The address and the approximate hour, about ten in the evening, come from a modern correspondence-based reconstruction and the hour remains uncorroborated. fr.wikipedia records the death in the ancien 2e arrondissement, which contained the quartier du Faubourg-Montmartre, so record and address agree. The coordinate is geocoded to number 9 against the French national address base, correcting an earlier value that sat mid-street near numbers 27 to 30.
stops.campa: He dies at number 9, rue du Faubourg-Montmartre, about ten at night, six weeks after the last book, at sixty-four years old. The disciples record a deathbed scene: the work unfinished, the succession arranged, the pear ripe and needing only to be picked. Whether he said any of that is a question about men who had every reason to remember him saying it. The street, the number and the hour are what the letters give, and the letters were not published for two hundred years.
suggested_refs: Pierre Musso, ed., Saint-Simon: Correspondance 1782-1825 (Manucius, 2025), source of the address and the hour
sources: Research dossier, citing Musso's correspondence-based reconstruction
api-adresse.data.gouv.fr geocoding of 9 rue du Faubourg Montmartre, 75009 Paris

stops.name: Pere-Lachaise, the civil funeral
stops.date_confidence: attested. The Association des Amis et Passionnes du Pere-Lachaise records the civil funeral of 22 May 1825, the family's absence, the grave in Division 28 along the chemin Camille-Jordan first line, reference M=Q-28, and the inscription. Attendance lists vary among later accounts and should not be read as an official roll. The coordinate is the corpus pin for the cemetery; a competing value of 2.3956 drifts east of Division 28 and is not used.
stops.campa: There is no priest. The funeral on the twenty-second of May is civil, the family stays away, and the men walking behind the coffin are the ones who worked for him: Olinde Rodrigues, Auguste Comte, Augustin Thierry, Prosper Enfantin, Leon Halevy. He goes into Division 28 along the chemin Camille-Jordan. The stone that eventually stands there reads Claude-Henri, Rouvroy, de Saint-Simon, economiste, 1760-1825, one profession out of the six he practised. The later accounts of who walked behind the coffin do not agree with one another.
suggested_refs: The grave in Division 28, chemin Camille-Jordan, Pere-Lachaise, and its inscription
sources: Wikipedia and New World Encyclopedia (burial at Pere-Lachaise)

stops.name: Paris, Le Producteur
stops.date_confidence: attested. Per fr.wikipedia's account of Saint-simonisme, Rodrigues proposes the journal at the funeral itself, the articles of partnership are signed 1 June 1825, the first issue appears 1 October 1825, and publication ceases in October 1826. Dated here to the first issue rather than to the conception or the partnership.
stops.campa: At the graveside Rodrigues proposes a journal. The articles of partnership are signed on the first of June, with Rodrigues and Prosper Enfantin as managing partners and Jacques Laffitte, Guillaume Louis Ternaux and Leon Halevy putting up the money. On the first of October the first number of Le Producteur appears under a motto taken from the dead man: the golden age, which a blind tradition has placed until now in the past, is before us. It runs for one year and stops.
suggested_refs: Le Producteur, Paris, 1 October 1825 to October 1826, and its epigraph on the golden age

stops.name: Paris, the disciples make the canon
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1832 Librairie Saint-Simonienne edition and for the textual history of the Parable, constituted as a standalone piece by that edition rather than by Saint-Simon in 1819. Month and day defaulted. Later reception noted in the refs below postdates the file's own clock and is recorded there rather than in the narrative.
stops.campa: Olinde Rodrigues publishes the posthumous anthology, prefaced by fragments of a life story written by the dead man himself, and in doing so settles which Saint-Simon there is going to be: the Geneva letters, the Parable, the Nouveau Christianisme, and not the forty years of pamphlets nobody bought. Everything argued afterwards in his name is argued out of this volume. The Parable becomes a standalone text here, seven years after his death, having never once been printed as one in his lifetime.
stops.quote: Already in his Geneva letters, Saint-Simon lays down the proposition that 'all men ought to work'.
stops.quote_source: Friedrich Engels, Socialism: Utopian and Scientific (1880), Part I, marxists.org. The words inside the quotation marks are Engels compressing the 1803 Lettres d'un habitant de Geneve, not a translated primary sentence of Saint-Simon's.
suggested_refs: Olinde Rodrigues, ed., Oeuvres de Saint-Simon, Librairie Saint-Simonienne, 1832, with 'Fragmens de l'histoire de sa vie ecrite par lui-meme'
